newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Stock suspension stirs Taiwan OTC controversy.
newsitem.headline: Stock suspension stirs Taiwan OTC controversy.

text.p: Taiwan's young over-the-counter exchange pledged on Wednesday to carry out its first suspension of a laggard firm's stock despite investor complaints that its "sudden death" disciplinary system was unfair.

An OTC official said the exchange notified the Securities and Exchange Commission that it had received formal notice from banks complaining of financial problems at corn oils processor Cheng-I Food Co and intended to halt trading of its shares.
"We received notice that Cheng-I indeed had bounced cheques so we will suspend the company's stock," an OTC official told Reuters by telephone.
The watchdog commission must approve the suspension.
The action against Cheng-I, the first suspension of any share by the fledgling over-the-counter exchange, would take effect by the end of December, the official said.
The disciplinary move has sparked an investor backlash.

Unlike the island's main Taiwan Stock Exchange, which can downgrade a stock to two lower levels before suspension, the OTC has a "sudden death" system in which trading is stopped as soon as financial problems surface.
In theory, Cheng-I could apply to resume trading within six months under OTC rules if it puts its financial house in order, but in reality a delisting after six months is all but certain.

Taiwan banks normally freeze a customer's credit line for three years after defaults or other serious financial problems, ensuring that the sanction will still be in place at the end of the OTC's six-month grace period.
"We have received a lot of investors complaints that the system is unfair," the OTC official said.
Banks imposed a three-year freeze on Cheng-I's access to credit in November after it bounced a series of cheques worth more than T$50 million.
The Securities and Exchange Commission, asked to comment on the OTC suspension rules, said the exchange was still evolving.
"The OTC is a new market so in the process of developing a trading system they should apply to us for any necessary regulatory changes," a commission official said by telephone.
After months of trials the OTC launched officially in September 1995, pioneering a new margin-based trading system, and has seen turnover climb steadily.
Turnover on November 25 surged to a one-day record of T$10.42 billion, which surpassed a tenth of the turnover on the main stock exchange that day, although volume has slowed in December.
The commission official would not comment on Cheng-I Food or say whether the suspension sought by the OTC would be authorised.
Cheng-I's stock has fluctuated wildly since news of its problems broke, both rising and falling by the OTC's seven percent daily limit on several occasions.
Food industry analysts and financial media have said Cheng-I had more than T$700 million in outstanding short-term liabilities.
Cheng-I is a major corn processor with registered capital of T$5.5 billion and estimated imports of about 630,000 tonnes of corn a year before the credit freeze halted its imports.
It sells a popular brand of corn oil in Taiwan.
